title: Speak It Into Existence
author: Dr. Chris Hobbs
summary: Dr. Chris Hobbs, a Christian school leader, argues that leaders can shape a school's identity by being deliberate about the words they use, grounding the idea in the image of God and the power of the tongue in Proverbs. Citing Al Mohler, he says every leader is eventually handed a microphone and that communication is leadership. He illustrates with a photographer who remarked that the language is so distinct at his school, and with elementary chapel where children recite pledges, Scripture and the mission. He offers five practices: clarify your words, place them where people will meet them, recite them in regular rhythms, tell stories about them, and reinforce them in annual reviews, drawing on Patrick Lencioni and Ruth Haley Barton. A pastor's remark that his congregation "kinda spoke it into existence" closes the piece. The central claim is that consistency, repetition and intentionality in language bring clarity to stakeholders and turn vision into reality.
points: Hobbs treats communication as part of leadership itself, so a leader who is not communicating clearly is not leading.
A school's distinct, consistent language, noticed even by an outside photographer, is presented as evidence that repeated words shape identity.
Five practices structure the advice: clarify, place, recite, tell stories about, and reinforce the school's key words.
Annual reviews are suggested as a place to measure staff against mission, core values or a portrait of a graduate, so that actions align with stated words.
Recitation and liturgical rhythms such as chapel and announcements are described as heart-shaping habits that should carry Scripture.
quotes: Dr. Al Mohler has a wonderful quote: “At some point, every leader is handed a microphone, and when that moment happens, the leader better have something to say.
Communication is leadership. Yet we rarely pause to consider what we should communicate, or how.
Our words matter. They are powerful. Used strategically, they make us distinctive to visitors, bring clarity to stakeholders, shape students’ hearts, and help turn vision into reality.
Patrick Lencioni ranks creating clarity as the second most important discipline of a healthy organization, behind only a cohesive leadership team.
Regular rhythms of recitation and corporate reading hide these words in your people’s hearts.
Nothing confirms that your words are alive and well quite like testimony.
Annual reviews should allow each employee to reflect on their performance through the lens of your mission, core values, or portrait of a graduate.
Your school’s rhythms are already shaping hearts. Make sure they are shaping them with the right words.
